title: Quantum computing roundup: Still more technologies making waves
gist: Three silicon- and diamond-based qubit approaches advanced at once: HRL Laboratories demonstrated an 18-qubit spin system that eliminates microwave control entirely (and was acquired by IBM despite IBM's transmon bet), Delft built a 1.2-micrometer spin bus with ~98 percent transport fidelity, and Saxon Q is shipping room-temperature, rack-mounted 100-plus-qubit diamond systems with 99.9 percent gate fidelity. Scalability, not qubit count, remains the deciding variable.

themes.theme: The scaling question dominates qubit technology selection

insights.claim: Backers choose qubit technologies primarily on projected scalability, which is why some companies with only a handful of qubits still attract support while rivals already field thousands.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Qubit-count headlines are a poor ranking signal; the investable variable is manufacturability and control-system scaling, not today's device size.
insights.quote: So even as some technologies can now support thousands of qubits, some competitors are still working on a small handful of qubits—the companies behind them are convinced that they have the potential to scale more effectively.
insights.locator: So even as some technologies can now support thousands of qubits

insights.claim: Quantum dots holding single electrons can be built with the same manufacturing technology used for traditional processors, which is the one approach with a proven scaling track record.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Leverage on existing semiconductor fab capacity is the structural argument for spin qubits—ties quantum roadmaps to the incumbent chip supply chain.
insights.locator: One of those technologies involves quantum dots

themes.theme: HRL removes microwaves from the control stack

insights.claim: HRL Laboratories, the descendant of Howard Hughes' research program, published in Nature a spin-qubit design using three quantum dots per qubit where operations are performed purely by electronically controlling how much the three electrons' spins interact.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: An all-electronic control scheme sidesteps the microwave cabling that constrains cryostat scaling—one of the hardest physical limits on qubit count.
insights.locator: Flipping spins

insights.claim: Eliminating microwaves removes the need for large amounts of microwave-carrying cabling into the near-absolute-zero refrigeration system, addressing a core wiring bottleneck in cryogenic quantum systems.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Cryostat I/O density is a known scaling wall; any approach that reduces cabling per qubit has outsized leverage on system size.
insights.locator: To do operations on this kind of qubit

insights.claim: HRL's control processor sits at an intermediate refrigeration level, consumes under 3.5 watts despite being built on a 130 nm process, runs autonomously after instructions are loaded, and communicates with the qubit chip via a superconducting ribbon cable.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Sub-4W cryo-CMOS on an ancient node implies large headroom from process migration—a cheap, near-term scaling lever.
insights.locator: HRL spends much of the paper describing its control system

insights.claim: HRL's 18-qubit system ran a simple error-correction code with a logical error rate below 1 percent, well behind other technologies but enough to indicate the remaining problems are engineering rather than physics.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The physics-versus-engineering distinction is the key de-risking marker for quantum investment; engineering problems have predictable capital and time curves.
insights.locator: The system HRL describes had 18 qubits

insights.claim: IBM acquired the company behind the HRL work even though IBM has bet big on transmon qubits controlled by exactly the microwave pulses HRL was trying to avoid.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: The incumbent buying a technology that undercuts its own control architecture is the clearest sign that modality risk is still live at the top of the field.
insights.locator: Hybrid machines

insights.claim: IBM Director of Research Jay Gambetta framed the rationale as a shared silicon foundation, since both superconducting qubits and spin qubits are built on silicon, giving IBM flexibility to run both programs in parallel.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Silicon as the common substrate lets a single capex base support multiple modality bets—an argument for concentration among firms with fab-scale infrastructure.
insights.quote: At a high level, I’m a strong believer in silicon technology—superconducting qubits are built on silicon, spins are built on silicon,
insights.locator: It’s not an obvious fit at first

insights.claim: Gambetta suggested a future IBM system could mix HRL spin technology alongside IBM's existing transmons, because different error-correction codes are better suited to memory versus magic state creation.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous quantum architectures—specialized qubit types for specialized roles—would mirror the CPU/GPU/accelerator split and reshape the competitive map.
insights.quote: I want to have the flexibility to build my hardware that maximizes both of them.
insights.locator: As we look at the error correction codes going forward

insights.claim: IBM has typically released a new processor architecture every year, refining it over two or three generations before moving on.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: A published cadence gives a concrete checkpoint schedule for judging whether IBM's roadmap claims are being met.
insights.locator: Right now, that foundation allows rapid iteration

insights.claim: Manufactured qubits have connections dictated by chip wiring, and since error-correction codes depend on connection geometry, fabricating a chip commits you to one or a few codes until the next hardware generation.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Code lock-in at tape-out is an underappreciated obsolescence risk for solid-state quantum hardware—an argument for slower capital commitment.
insights.locator: One problem with quantum dots and other manufactured qubits

insights.claim: Trapped-ion and neutral-atom qubits avoid this because any qubit can be moved to connect with any other, and their backers expect that algorithmic flexibility to outweigh their slower operations versus silicon.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Frames the core modality tradeoff—speed versus connectivity—that determines which architectures win which workloads.
insights.locator: Qubits based on trapped ions or neutral atoms

insights.claim: Delft University of Technology showed spins can be shuttled through several intervening quantum dots to the opposite side of a chip, combining silicon manufacturability with the arbitrary-connectivity advantage of atom-based systems.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: If spin shuttling scales, the manufacturability-versus-flexibility tradeoff collapses in silicon's favor—the single biggest potential modality shift here.
insights.locator: In May, however, the Delft team showed

insights.claim: Delft's new paper builds an electron bus with storage 'bus stops', reporting a 1.2 micrometer route with nearly 98 percent fidelity for sending a spin end-to-end and back.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: 98 percent round-trip transport fidelity is the concrete number to track against future generations—it must climb sharply before error-corrected use.
insights.locator: Wednesday’s paper expands on that

insights.claim: Delft's error characterization traced most error to two sources: noise arising during the spin exchanges needed for entanglement, and loss of coherence while qubits are moved or idling.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Named, localized error sources are what turn a research demo into an engineering roadmap—watch these two metrics in follow-on papers.
insights.locator: They also characterize the sources of error

themes.theme: Room-temperature diamond qubits from Saxon Q

insights.claim: Nitrogen-vacancy diamond qubits stalled for a decade because nitrogen placement could not be controlled, forcing every chip to be bespoke rather than standardized.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Explains why the modality was written off—and why a placement breakthrough is the specific thing that reopens it.
insights.locator: Diamonds are a qubit’s best friend?

insights.claim: Saxon Q, a spinout of Universität Leipzig, has apparently developed a technique to place nitrogen vacancies within a 10-nanometer radius, enabling standardized chip layouts.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Deterministic defect placement is the unlock for manufacturable NV-diamond hardware—a modality that had been counted out.
insights.locator: Saxon Q, a spinout of the Universität Leipzig

insights.claim: Saxon Q's hardware runs at room temperature, fits in a standard rack mount, and plugs into a normal power supply—eliminating the cryogenic infrastructure that dominates the cost and footprint of competing systems.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Removing the dilution refrigerator changes the deployment economics entirely—quantum as rack-mounted datacenter equipment rather than a lab installation.
insights.locator: The company’s hardware is striking in several ways

insights.claim: Saxon Q builds modular eight-qubit 'cores' that can be combined in a single rack, announced units with over 100 qubits total, and expects shipping within a few months with larger systems next year.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Modular core aggregation is a commercially familiar scaling story—easier to finance and forecast than monolithic chip scaling.
insights.locator: the company builds a “core” with eight qubits

insights.claim: Saxon Q claims individual hardware qubit gate fidelity above 99.9 percent, competitive with others on the market, though both its current and near-term systems will be too small for interesting error-corrected computation.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: High fidelity at small scale is necessary but not sufficient—the honest read is optionality, not near-term revenue.
